questions.stem: According to the wounded Captain, what did Macbeth do to the rebel Macdonwald?
options: Captured him and sent him to Duncan for trial
Drove him back by sea to the Western Isles
Split him open and set his head on the battlements
Wounded him and let him flee to the Norwegian camp
questions.why: The Captain reports that Macbeth cut Macdonwald open "from the nave to the chops" and fixed his head on the battlements; the rebel was neither captured nor allowed to escape.

questions.stem: Macbeth's first words in the play are "So foul and fair a day I have not seen." What makes this line unsettling in context?
options: It echoes the witches' chant before he has ever met them
It repeats the Captain's words to Duncan about the battle
It mocks Banquo, who has just complained about the storm
It answers the greeting the witches have just given him
questions.why: In Scene 1 the witches chant "Fair is foul, and foul is fair"; Macbeth unknowingly echoes them in Scene 3 before they speak to him. They have not yet greeted him (D), and Banquo speaks only after this line (C).

checkpoint.question: When Duncan embraces Banquo at Forres and holds him to his heart, what does Banquo say will be Duncan's own if he grows there?
checkpoint.evidence: There if I grow, The harvest is your own.

questions.stem: Soon after Nick moves to West Egg, what makes him stop feeling lonely?
options: His Finnish housekeeper starts cooking his evening meals
A newcomer stops him on the road to ask the way to West Egg village
A young man from his office moves into the bungalow with him
Daisy telephones to invite him to dinner in East Egg
questions.why: Being asked for directions makes Nick feel like a settler; the coworker who found the house was sent to Washington, so Nick moved in alone.

questions.stem: As Nick starts his car to leave, Daisy calls him back: "I forgot to ask you something, and it's important." What does the "important" matter turn out to be, and what does it show?
options: A rumor that Nick is engaged out West, showing how the Buchanans feed on gossip
Whether Nick knows his neighbor Gatsby, showing her hidden interest in him
Whether Nick will keep quiet about Tom's call, showing her fear of scandal
Whether Nick will bring Jordan home from her tournament, showing her matchmaking
questions.why: The 'important' question is only a rumor that Nick is engaged out West, which Daisy believes because 'three people' repeated it; the urgent tone set against a trivial piece of gossip shows how the Buchanans live on hearsay.

checkpoint.question: According to Daisy Buchanan, where is Jordan Baker going to play in the golf tournament the day after the dinner?
checkpoint.evidence: “Jordan’s going to play in the tournament tomorrow,” explained Daisy, “over at Westchester.”

questions.stem: According to Walton's first letter, what kept him from going to sea as a boy?
options: His sister Margaret's fear that he would drown on a voyage
His father's dying wish, which forbade his uncle to let him go
His uncle Thomas's own refusal to let him leave school
A weak constitution that left him unfit for hard labor
questions.why: B: the father's dying injunction bound the uncle; uncle Thomas only supplied the books of voyages, so C reverses who forbade it.

questions.stem: In Letter IV, Walton writes of the stranger: "Such a man has a double existence." In context, what are the two sides of this existence?
options: His former life as a scholar and his present life as a hunter on the ice
Misery on one side; on the other, a soul raised by nature like a haloed spirit
His gentle courtesy toward Walton and his fierce hatred for the one he pursues
A strong, wise mind trapped inside a body ruined by cold, hunger and fatigue
questions.why: B: the line follows Walton's remark that the starry sky and sea still elevate the stranger's soul; one existence suffers misery, the other, 'retired into himself', is 'like a celestial spirit' with a halo.

checkpoint.question: To what creature does the stranger compare the gratification of Captain Walton's wishes, warning that it may sting him?
checkpoint.evidence: You seek for knowledge and wisdom, as I once did; and I ardently hope that the gratification of your wishes may not be a serpent to sting you, as mine has been.

questions.stem: As Mr. Pontellier gets up to go to Klein's hotel, what does Edna hand him?
options: The white sunshade she and Robert had walked under from the beach
The newspaper he had left lying on the porch step
A list of the things the boys wanted from the hotel
Her sister's letter, to be mailed from the hotel
questions.why: Edna holds out the umbrella, the pink-lined white sunshade she and Robert walked under, and he carries it off over his head. She reads her sister's letter only later, with Robert.

questions.stem: On the porch after midnight, Edna hears only an owl and "the everlasting voice of the sea, that was not uplifted at that soft hour." To what does the next sentence compare that voice, and what does the comparison add?
options: A distant church bell, calling Edna back to her duties
A lover's whisper, hinting at her feelings for Robert
A scolding voice, echoing her husband's reproaches
A mournful lullaby, soothing and sorrowful at once, like her tears
questions.why: The sea "broke like a mournful lullaby upon the night": a lullaby comforts, "mournful" grieves, and the double note matches Edna crying without knowing why.

checkpoint.question: What game are the little Pontellier children playing under the oaks while Edna Pontellier and Robert Lebrun chat on the porch?
checkpoint.evidence: They chatted incessantly: about the things around them; their amusing adventure out in the water—it had again assumed its entertaining aspect; about the wind, the trees, the people who had gone to the _Chênière;_ about the children playing croquet under the oaks, and the Farival twins, who were now performing the overture to “The Poet and the Peasant.”

questions.stem: In Scene 1, the Ghost returns and Horatio begs it to speak. What happens just as it seems about to answer?
options: Barnardo cries out and frightens it away
The bell strikes one and it falls silent
A cock crows and it starts away
Hamlet arrives and it turns toward him
questions.why: Barnardo says the Ghost "was about to speak, when the cock crew," and Horatio describes it starting "like a guilty thing"; Hamlet is not on the platform in Scene 1.

questions.stem: Just after the Ghost leaves him, Marcellus calls out to Hamlet from offstage, and Hamlet answers, "Hillo, ho, ho, boy! Come, bird, come." What does this reply show in context?
options: He is calling the Ghost to come back and finish its tale
He is warning his friends to keep away from the Ghost
He is signaling Horatio to come alone, without Marcellus
He echoes their halloo like a falconer, in a strange, giddy mood
questions.why: Marcellus's cry "Illo, ho, ho, my lord!" is answered with a falconer's call to his hawk. Shaken by what the Ghost has told him, Hamlet turns playful and evasive, and Horatio soon calls his talk "wild and whirling words." The Ghost has already gone, and Hamlet asks both men to join him.

checkpoint.question: While waiting on the platform for the Ghost, what wine does Hamlet say King Claudius drains as the kettle-drum and trumpet bray out?
checkpoint.evidence: The King doth wake tonight and takes his rouse, Keeps wassail, and the swaggering upspring reels; And as he drains his draughts of Rhenish down, The kettle-drum and trumpet thus bray out The triumph of his pledge.

questions.stem: While he is Surveyor, the narrator says his name now has "another kind of vogue" and travels where it had never been before. How does it travel?
options: Printed in the shipping lists of the Salem newspaper
Stenciled in black paint on pepper-bags and cigar-boxes
Signed at the foot of every sailor's protection paper
Engraved on a brass plate beside the Custom-House door
questions.why: No longer on title-pages, his name is stenciled in black paint on dutiable goods that have paid the impost, an ironic "queer vehicle of fame" for a writer.

questions.stem: While the narrator paces the Custom-House brooding, the old officers comment: "Remembering their own former habits, they used to say that the Surveyor was walking the quarter-deck." What does this remark show in context?
options: They resent his pacing as a sign he will drive them like a crew
They honor him as a fellow captain who has commanded at sea
They take his restless thinking for an old sailor's walk for appetite
They mock him as a landsman pretending to know the ways of ships
questions.why: The retired sea-captains can only read his pacing through their own habits: a shipmaster's walk, done to get an appetite for dinner. They have no idea he is brooding over Hester's story; they are annoyed, not honored or mocking.

checkpoint.question: How many children had the old Inspector of the Custom-House fathered with his three long-dead wives?
checkpoint.evidence: He had been the husband of three wives, all long since dead; the father of twenty children, most of whom, at every age of childhood or maturity, had likewise returned to dust.

questions.stem: In Chapter 1, when Heathcliff's dogs attack Lockwood, a woman rushes in from the kitchen and drives them off. What does she use as her weapon?
options: The poker from the hearth
A frying-pan
A pail of icy water
A heavy walking-stick
questions.why: The "lusty dame" from the kitchen routs the dogs with a frying-pan and her tongue. The poker is what Lockwood himself used to fend them off, and the icy water comes later, from Zillah in Chapter 2.

questions.stem: Lockwood recalls offering to help young Mrs. Heathcliff: "she turned upon me as a miser might turn if any one attempted to assist him in counting his gold." In context, what is she doing, and what does the comparison show?
options: Reaching for the tea canisters, she guards even this small task as her own
Counting the household money, she suspects Lockwood means to rob her
Opening her book of the Black Art, she hides it from a stranger's eyes
Feeding Juno's puppies, she refuses to let a guest touch the dogs
questions.why: She is only reaching for the painted tea canisters on the chimney-piece, yet she snaps at Lockwood's offer as if he were after her gold: she fiercely guards the little that is hers in that house. The Black Art book comes later, to frighten Joseph, and she says the puppies are "not mine."

checkpoint.question: In the parlour at Wuthering Heights, what lies on the cushion that Mr. Lockwood mistakes for a heap of cats?
checkpoint.evidence: Unluckily, it was a heap of dead rabbits.

questions.stem: When Jane comes out from behind the curtain, John Reed sits in an arm-chair and makes her stand before him. What does he spend some three minutes doing before he strikes her?
options: Reading aloud mockingly from her book of birds
Thrusting out his tongue at her as far as he can
Eating sweetmeats and refusing to share them
Listing every fault his mother has found in her
questions.why: Jane stands before his chair while he spends "some three minutes" thrusting out his tongue; then he strikes "suddenly and strongly." He has not yet seen the book (A); the sweetmeats (C) belong only to the narrator's account of his schooling.

questions.stem: A light gleams on the red-room wall, and Jane wonders: "Was it, I asked myself, a ray from the moon penetrating some aperture in the blind? No; moonlight was still, and this stirred." In context, how does the adult narrator later account for the light?
options: As firelight caught in the great looking-glass
As a gleam from a lantern carried across the lawn
As a candle carried along the passage by Bessie
As lightning from the storm still raging outside
questions.why: Looking back, the narrator conjectures it was "a gleam from a lantern carried by some one across the lawn"; the frightened child took it for a herald from another world. The room has no fire (A), and Bessie comes only after the scream (C).

checkpoint.question: What does Bessie ask Miss Abbot to lend her, to tie Jane Eyre down on the stool in the red-room?
checkpoint.evidence: “Miss Abbot, lend me your garters; she would break mine directly.”
